Phil Flanigan is one of the most in-demand bassists in jazz today. A native of Geneva, New York, he found fertile playing ground in Providence with tenor saxophonist Scott Hamilton. With guitarist Chris Flory and drummer Chuck Riggs, a working quartet evolved that eventually recorded over twenty albums and helped renew interest in mainstream jazz. In New York, Phil performed and recorded with a long list of jazz veterans including Bob Wilber, Benny Goodman, Mel Torme and Maxine Sullivan. His passion is preserving the acoustic quality of the bass in jazz and he has demonstrated that conviction on over fifty recordings to date. Phil travels from his home in Florida to appear at festivals and jazz parties here and abroad. His most recent solo release is entitled “New York Toast” and features his original compositions for quartet.
Phil was interviewed in San Diego, California on February 15, 1998, by Monk Rowe, Director of the Fillius Jazz Archive.

My name is Monk Rowe and we are filming in San Diego, California at the San Diego Jazz Party and it’s a real pleasure to have bassist Phil Flanigan with me, one of the fine upstate New York jazz musicians on the scene today. But you’re one of the few whose name does not end with a vowel you know.
Well that depends on how many other upstate musicians you’re aware of.
Well why don’t you fill me in, because there’s probably all sorts that I don’t know about.

Well the immediate few that come to mind are my contemporaries in Geneva, in years probably ‘72 to ‘74, Michael Hashim, the alto saxophonist, and Chris Flory the guitarist, also with Scott Hamilton. His original home is Geneva also. And a drummer by the name of John Ellis in New York. Those are just Genevans. And I’ve become more aware of other upstaters like Mel Lewis and Lonnie Smith the organist — they’re Buffalo guys. and then of course all the other Italian upstate guys, the Joe Romanos and the Scott LaFaros.
